notes.front: What is a version control system (VCS)?
notes.back: A system that tracks the history of changes as people and teams collaborate on a project.
notes.explanation: As developers change the project, any earlier version of it can be recovered at any time.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git”, “About version control and Git”
notes.evidence: A version control system, or VCS, tracks the history of changes as people and teams collaborate on projects together. As developers make changes to the project, any earlier version of the project can be recovered at any time.
notes.example: Like the undo history in a word processor, but shared by the whole team and kept for the life of the project.

notes.front: What is a distributed version control system (DVCS)?
notes.back: A version control system in which every developer has a full copy of the project and its history.
notes.explanation: The GitHub docs contrast it with the once popular centralised systems: a DVCS does not need a constant connection to a central repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git”, “About version control and Git”
notes.evidence: In a distributed version control system, every developer has a full copy of the project and project history. Unlike once popular centralized version control systems, DVCSs don't need a constant connection to a central repository.
notes.example: Like every member of a choir holding the full score, rather than one conductor holding the only copy.

notes.front: What is Git?
notes.back: A version control system that tracks changes to files.
notes.explanation: Git lets you work on your own copy of a project, record a history of your changes and merge your work with other people's safely.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “What is GitHub?”, “GitHub and Git”
notes.evidence: Git is a version control system that tracks changes to files. It lets you work on your own copy of a project, record a history of your changes, and merge your work with other people's changes safely.
notes.example: A developer records each change to a small website on their laptop with Git, with no website or server involved.

notes.front: What is GitHub?
notes.back: A platform that hosts Git repositories and gives developers tools to ship better code.
notes.explanation: Its tools include command line features, issues, pull requests, code review and apps from the GitHub Marketplace, among others.
notes.evidence: GitHub hosts Git repositories and provides developers with tools to ship better code through command line features, issues (threaded discussions), pull requests, code review, or the use of a collection of free and for-purchase apps in the GitHub Marketplace.
notes.example: A team keeps its Git project on GitHub so that everyone can see it, discuss it and review changes in a browser.

notes.front: In Git, what is a repository?
notes.back: The entire collection of files and folders for a project, along with each file's revision history.
notes.explanation: The docs also call it a Git project; its history appears as commits, which can be organised into branches.
notes.evidence: A repository, or Git project, encompasses the entire collection of files and folders associated with a project, along with each file's revision history. The file history appears as snapshots in time called commits. The commits can be organized into multiple lines of development called branches.
notes.example: Like a project folder, but one that also remembers every earlier state of every file in it.

notes.front: In a Git repository, what is a commit?
notes.back: A snapshot in time of the repository's files; the file history is made of commits.
notes.explanation: Commits make up a repository's file history, and they can be organised into branches.
notes.evidence: The file history appears as snapshots in time called commits. The commits can be organized into multiple lines of development called branches.
notes.example: Like saving a numbered photo of your whole project each time you finish a small piece of work.

notes.front: In a Git repository, what is a branch?
notes.back: A line of development: commits can be organised into multiple branches.
notes.explanation: A repository can hold several branches, each its own line of development.
notes.evidence: The commits can be organized into multiple lines of development called branches.
notes.example: Like drafting a new chapter in a copy of a manuscript while the published version stays untouched.

notes.front: What is a clone?
notes.back: A copy of a repository that lives on your computer rather than on a server, or the act of making that copy.
notes.explanation: With a clone you can edit files and use Git to track your changes without being online.
notes.evidence: A clone is a copy of a repository that lives on your computer instead of on a website's server somewhere, or the act of making that copy. When you make a clone, you can edit the files in your preferred editor and use Git to keep track of your changes without having to be online.
notes.example: Like downloading a shared folder with its full history, so you can keep working on a flight.

notes.front: In the GitHub glossary, what is a remote?
notes.back: The version of a repository or branch that is hosted on a server, most likely GitHub.com.
notes.explanation: Remote versions can be connected to local clones so that changes can be synced.
notes.evidence: This is the version of a repository or branch that is hosted on a server, most likely GitHub.com. Remote versions can be connected to local clones so that changes can be synced.
notes.example: The copy of a team's project on GitHub.com is the remote for each teammate's laptop copy.

notes.front: In Git, what does it mean to push?
notes.back: To send your committed changes to a remote repository, for example on GitHub.com.
notes.explanation: Pushing lets others access changes you made locally.
notes.evidence: To push means to send your committed changes to a remote repository on GitHub.com. For instance, if you change something locally, you can push those changes so that others may access them.
notes.example: Like uploading the pages you have finished so co-authors can read them.

notes.front: What does git fetch do?
notes.back: It adds changes from the remote repository to your local working branch without committing them.
notes.explanation: Unlike git pull, fetching lets you review the changes before committing them to your local branch.
notes.evidence: When you use `git fetch`, you're adding changes from the remote repository to your local working branch without committing them. Unlike `git pull`, fetching allows you to review changes before committing them to your local branch.
notes.example: Like collecting your post and reading it before deciding what to file.

notes.front: In Git, what does merging do?
notes.back: It takes the changes from one branch and applies them into another.
notes.explanation: The source branch can be in the same repository or in a fork; merging often happens through a pull request or on the command line.
notes.evidence: Merging takes the changes from one branch (in the same repository or from a fork), and applies them into another. This often happens as a “pull request” (which can be thought of as a request to merge), or via the command line.
notes.example: Like folding the edits from a draft chapter back into the main manuscript.

notes.front: In Git, what does pull mean?
notes.back: Fetching in changes and merging them.
notes.explanation: You pull when someone has edited the remote file you are both working on and you want your local copy up to date.
notes.evidence: Pull refers to when you are fetching in changes and merging them. For instance, if someone has edited the remote file you're both working on, you'll want to pull in those changes to your local copy so that it's up to date.
notes.example: Like collecting your post and filing it straight away, without reading it first.

notes.front: As developers change a project under version control, any {{c1::earlier version}} of the project can be recovered at any time.
notes.back: earlier version
notes.explanation: A VCS tracks the history of changes as people and teams collaborate on a project.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git”, “About version control and Git”
notes.evidence: A version control system, or VCS, tracks the history of changes as people and teams collaborate on projects together. As developers make changes to the project, any earlier version of the project can be recovered at any time.

notes.front: Reviewing project history answers several questions. In the GitHub docs' wording, which question asks about the content of the changes?
notes.back: Which changes were made?
notes.explanation: Project history can tell developers which changes were made, who made them, when, and why.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git”, “About version control and Git”
notes.evidence: Which changes were made?

notes.front: Reviewing project history answers several questions. In the GitHub docs' wording, which question asks about authorship?
notes.back: Who made the changes?
notes.explanation: Project history can tell developers which changes were made, who made them, when, and why.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git”, “About version control and Git”
notes.evidence: Who made the changes?

notes.front: Reviewing project history answers several questions. In the GitHub docs' wording, which question asks about timing?
notes.back: When were the changes made?
notes.explanation: Project history can tell developers which changes were made, who made them, when, and why.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git”, “About version control and Git”
notes.evidence: When were the changes made?

notes.front: Reviewing project history answers several questions. In the GitHub docs' wording, which question asks about the reason for the changes?
notes.back: Why were changes needed?
notes.explanation: Project history can tell developers which changes were made, who made them, when, and why.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git”, “About version control and Git”
notes.evidence: Why were changes needed?

notes.front: How does a distributed version control system differ from the once popular centralised systems in its need for a connection?
notes.back: A DVCS does not need a constant connection to a central repository.
notes.explanation: In a DVCS every developer has a full copy of the project and its history.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git”, “About version control and Git”
notes.evidence: In a distributed version control system, every developer has a full copy of the project and project history. Unlike once popular centralized version control systems, DVCSs don't need a constant connection to a central repository.

notes.front: Git is the most popular {{c1::distributed version control system}}.
notes.back: distributed version control system
notes.explanation: The docs add that Git is commonly used for both open source and commercial software development.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git”, “About version control and Git”
notes.evidence: Git is the most popular distributed version control system. Git is commonly used for both open source and commercial software development

notes.front: Because Git is a DVCS, what can anyone who has a copy of a repository access?
notes.back: The entire codebase and its history.
notes.explanation: The docs describe Git repositories as self-contained units for this reason.
notes.evidence: Because Git is a DVCS, repositories are self-contained units and anyone who has a copy of the repository can access the entire codebase and its history.

notes.front: Priya is on a long flight with no internet. She wants to record several commits on her project and look back through its full history. Which kind of version control makes this possible?
notes.back: C: a distributed version control system such as Git, because her copy holds the full project and history.
notes.explanation: In a DVCS every developer has a full copy of the project and its history, and no constant connection to a central repository is needed.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git”, “About version control and Git”
notes.evidence: In a distributed version control system, every developer has a full copy of the project and project history. Unlike once popular centralized version control systems, DVCSs don't need a constant connection to a central repository.
notes.choices:
A) Neither: all version control needs a live server
B) A centralised version control system
C) A distributed version control system such as Git
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the docs contrast centralised systems with DVCSs, which don't need a constant connection to a central repository. C is wrong: a DVCS gives each developer a full local copy of the history.

notes.front: A page on a team's site broke last week. The lead wants to know which change caused it, who made it, when, and why it was made. Where should she look?
notes.back: C: the project history kept by their version control system.
notes.explanation: A VCS tracks the history of changes, and developers can review that history to find out which changes were made, who made them, when and why.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git”, “About version control and Git”
notes.evidence: Developers can review project history to find out: * Which changes were made? * Who made the changes? * When were the changes made? * Why were changes needed?
notes.choices:
A) Nowhere: once a change is made, earlier versions are lost
B) Only the current version of the files
C) The project history in their version control system
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the current files show the result, not who changed them, when or why. C is wrong: under version control any earlier version can be recovered at any time.

notes.front: Lena joins a project and gets a copy of its Git repository. Can she see how the code looked a year ago?
notes.back: C: yes, her copy holds the entire codebase and its history.
notes.explanation: Git repositories are self-contained units, so anyone with a copy can access the entire codebase and its history.
notes.evidence: Because Git is a DVCS, repositories are self-contained units and anyone who has a copy of the repository can access the entire codebase and its history.
notes.choices:
A) Only while connected to a central server
B) No: only the latest files are copied
C) Yes: her copy holds the entire codebase and history
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: a Git repository includes each file's revision history. C is wrong: a DVCS doesn't need a constant connection to a central repository.

notes.front: Omar wants to try a risky change to a live product's code and let colleagues look at it, without touching the production code yet. What should he work on?
notes.back: C: a branch.
notes.explanation: Branches let developers safely propose changes to production code.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git”, “About version control and Git”
notes.evidence: Using branches, developers can safely propose changes to production code.
notes.choices:
A) A new, unrelated repository
B) The production code directly
C) A branch
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: editing production code directly is what he wants to avoid. C is wrong: a branch keeps the change inside the same repository as another line of development.

notes.front: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
notes.back: Git is the version control system; GitHub hosts Git repositories in the cloud and adds planning and collaboration tools.
notes.explanation: GitHub builds on Git rather than replacing it: it hosts Git projects and adds tools around them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “What is GitHub?”, “GitHub and Git”
notes.evidence: GitHub builds on Git by hosting your Git projects, called **repositories**, in the cloud, as well as adding planning and collaboration tools

notes.front: GitHub is based on the open-source software {{c1::Git}}.
notes.back: Git
notes.explanation: Git is the version control system that tracks changes to files; GitHub is built on it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “What is GitHub?”, “GitHub and Git”
notes.evidence: GitHub is based on the open-source software, Git. Git is a version control system that tracks changes to files.

notes.front: A team's code review, issue discussions and pull requests all happen in a web browser, while each developer records snapshots of their work locally. Which part is Git and which is GitHub?
notes.back: C: local snapshots are Git; the hosted review, issues and pull requests are GitHub.
notes.explanation: Git is the version control system that tracks changes; GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds tools such as issues, pull requests and code review.
notes.evidence: GitHub hosts Git repositories and provides developers with tools to ship better code through command line features, issues (threaded discussions), pull requests, code review
notes.choices:
A) Local snapshots are GitHub; the browser tools are Git
B) All of it is Git
C) Local snapshots are Git; hosted review, issues and pull requests are GitHub
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: issues, pull requests and code review are tools GitHub adds on top of Git. C swaps the two: Git tracks the changes, GitHub hosts the repositories.

notes.front: Besides the project's files and folders, what else does a Git repository hold?
notes.back: Each file's revision history.
notes.explanation: That history is stored as commits, the snapshots in time the docs describe.
notes.evidence: encompasses the entire collection of files and folders associated with a project, along with each file's revision history.

notes.front: According to the GitHub docs, what do branches let developers do safely?
notes.back: Propose changes to production code.
notes.explanation: The docs list this among the benefits Git brings to individuals, teams and businesses.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git”, “About version control and Git”
notes.evidence: Using branches, developers can safely propose changes to production code.

notes.front: Once you have a clone, what can you do without being online?
notes.back: Edit the files in your preferred editor and use Git to keep track of your changes.
notes.explanation: The clone stays connected to the remote version, so you can push your changes to keep them synced once you are back online.
notes.evidence: When you make a clone, you can edit the files in your preferred editor and use Git to keep track of your changes without having to be online. The repository you cloned is still connected to the remote version so that you can push your local changes to the remote to keep them synced when you're online.

notes.front: Tom cloned a repository from GitHub, made commits while offline and is now back online. How does he get his commits back to the version on GitHub?
notes.back: A: push his local changes to the remote.
notes.explanation: A clone is still connected to the remote version, so you can push local changes to keep them synced when you're online.
notes.evidence: The repository you cloned is still connected to the remote version so that you can push your local changes to the remote to keep them synced when you're online.
notes.choices:
A) Push his local changes to the remote
B) Fetch from the remote
C) Clone the repository again
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: fetching brings changes from the remote into his branch, not the other way. C is wrong: a fresh clone would copy the remote, which lacks his new commits.

notes.front: What can you do with git fetch that git pull does not give you the chance to do?
notes.back: Review the changes before committing them to your local branch.
notes.explanation: Fetching adds the remote changes to your local working branch without committing them.
notes.evidence: When you use `git fetch`, you're adding changes from the remote repository to your local working branch without committing them. Unlike `git pull`, fetching allows you to review changes before committing them to your local branch.

notes.front: A teammate has pushed commits to the shared branch. Aisha wants to look at them before they become part of her local branch. Which command suits her?
notes.back: C: git fetch.
notes.explanation: Fetching adds the remote changes to her working branch without committing them, so she can review them first.
notes.evidence: Unlike `git pull`, fetching allows you to review changes before committing them to your local branch.
notes.choices:
A) git push
B) git pull
C) git fetch
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: pull fetches and merges straight away, with no review step. C is wrong: push sends her own commits to the remote.

notes.front: Someone has edited a file on the remote that you are both working on, and you simply want your local copy brought up to date. What do you do?
notes.back: C: pull in those changes.
notes.explanation: Pull fetches the changes and merges them, which the glossary describes as the way to keep your local copy up to date.
notes.evidence: For instance, if someone has edited the remote file you're both working on, you'll want to pull in those changes to your local copy so that it's up to date.
notes.choices:
A) Make a new clone in another folder
B) Push your local copy
C) Pull in the changes
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: pushing sends your commits to the remote and does not bring theirs down. C is wrong: the glossary's answer is to pull into the copy you already have.

notes.front: When can a merge be done through the GitHub.com web interface, and when on the command line?
notes.back: Web interface: through a pull request, if there are no conflicting changes. Command line: always.
notes.explanation: The glossary notes that merges often happen as a pull request, which can be thought of as a request to merge.
notes.evidence: This often happens as a "pull request" (which can be thought of as a request to merge), or via the command line. A merge can be done through a pull request via the GitHub.com web interface if there are no conflicting changes, or can always be done via the command line.

notes.front: Which Git command initialises a brand new repository and begins tracking an existing directory?
notes.back: git init
notes.explanation: It adds a hidden subfolder that holds the internal data structure needed for version control.
notes.evidence: git init initializes a brand new Git repository and begins tracking an existing directory. It adds a hidden subfolder within the existing directory that houses the internal data structure required for version control.

notes.front: Which Git command creates a local copy of a project that already exists remotely, including all its files, history and branches?
notes.back: git clone
notes.explanation: It is for a project that already exists remotely; git init is the command that starts a brand new repository.
notes.evidence: git clone creates a local copy of a project that already exists remotely. The clone includes all the project's files, history, and branches.

notes.front: Which Git command stages a change, the first step of the two-step process of adding it to history?
notes.back: git add
notes.explanation: Staged changes become part of the next snapshot and part of the project's history.
notes.evidence: This command performs staging, the first part of that two-step process. Any changes that are staged will become a part of the next snapshot and a part of the project's history.

notes.front: Which Git command saves the staged snapshot to the project history and completes the change-tracking process?
notes.back: git commit
notes.explanation: The docs compare it to taking a photo of whatever was staged with git add.
notes.evidence: git commit saves the snapshot to the project history and completes the change-tracking process. In short, a commit functions like taking a photo.

notes.front: Which Git command shows whether changes are untracked, modified or staged?
notes.back: git status
notes.explanation: Those three states are the ones it reports: untracked, modified and staged.
notes.evidence: git status shows the status of changes as untracked, modified, or staged.

notes.front: Which Git command shows the branches being worked on locally?
notes.back: git branch
notes.explanation: Branches are the lines of development that commits are organised into.
notes.evidence: git branch shows the branches being worked on locally.

notes.front: Which Git command combines lines of development, typically changes made on two distinct branches?
notes.back: git merge
notes.explanation: For example, a developer merges a feature branch into the main branch for deployment.
notes.evidence: This command is typically used to combine changes made on two distinct branches. For example, a developer would merge when they want to combine changes from a feature branch into the main branch for deployment.

notes.front: Which Git command updates your local line of development with updates from its remote counterpart?
notes.back: git pull
notes.explanation: Developers use it when a teammate has made commits to a branch on a remote.
notes.evidence: git pull updates the local line of development with updates from its remote counterpart. Developers use this command if a teammate has made commits to a branch on a remote

notes.front: Which Git command updates the remote repository with commits made locally to a branch?
notes.back: git push
notes.explanation: It is how local commits reach the remote repository.
notes.evidence: git push updates the remote repository with any commits made locally to a branch.

notes.front: What are the two primary ways people collaborate on GitHub, and how does each give access?
notes.back: Shared repository: named contributors get read, write or administrator access. Fork and pull: anyone who can view the project can contribute.
notes.explanation: In the shared repository model, access is a simple permission structure of explicitly named contributors.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git”, “Models for collaborative development”
notes.evidence: There are two primary ways people collaborate on GitHub: 1. Shared repository 2. Fork and pull With a shared repository, individuals and teams are explicitly designated as contributors with read, write, or administrator access.

notes.front: An open source project wants anyone who can see it to be able to offer fixes, without the maintainers managing individual permissions. Which collaboration model fits?
notes.back: A: fork and pull.
notes.explanation: The docs say managing individual permissions can be challenging for such projects, but fork and pull allows anyone who can view the project to contribute.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Git”, “Models for collaborative development”
notes.evidence: For an open source project, or for projects to which anyone can contribute, managing individual permissions can be challenging, but a fork and pull model allows anyone who can view the project to contribute.
notes.choices:
A) Fork and pull
B) Shared repository
C) Neither: open source projects cannot take outside contributions
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: a shared repository needs contributors to be explicitly designated with access. C is wrong: fork and pull exists precisely to take such contributions.
